draft.title: Safety devices
card: Fuse
a thin wire in the live line that melts when the current is too high. This breaks the circuit. Once melted, it must be replaced.
Circuit breaker
a switch that trips open when the current is too high, so the circuit is broken. It can be reset after the fault is fixed.
Earthing

a wire joins the metal case of an appliance to the ground. If the live wire touches the case, current flows safely through the earth wire. This also makes a large current that blows the fuse or trips the breaker.
Residual current device
a device that compares the current in the live and neutral wires. If some current leaks out, as it would through a person, the two differ and it cuts the power very quickly.
draft.remember: Fuses and breakers stop too much current. Earthing gives a safe path. A residual current device spots leaks.

a.q: Which device cuts the power because the current in the live and neutral wires is different?
opts: A residual current device
A fuse
A circuit breaker
An earth wire
a.why: A residual current device compares the two currents, and a difference means current is leaking elsewhere. A fuse and a circuit breaker respond to a high current in the circuit, not to a difference between wires.

b.q: Jo's metal toaster has a fault, and the live wire touches its metal case. The case is earthed. What does the earth wire do?
opts: Carries current away, so the fuse blows or breaker trips
Stops any current flowing in the live wire
Lowers the voltage of the toaster's heating wire
Replaces the fuse so the toaster needs none
b.why: The earth wire gives the fault current an easy path to the ground. The large current melts the fuse or trips the breaker, which cuts the power and leaves the case safe. It does not replace the fuse: the fuse or breaker still does the cutting.
b.clue: Think about what a large fault current does to a fuse.

b.best: Carries current away, so the fuse blows or breaker trips

problems.detail: The right option is the longest and the only one with a two-step detail (current flows away, then the fuse blows or the breaker trips). The clue, 'Think about what a large fault current does to a fuse', also points straight to it, so a student could pick it without knowing what earthing does.

b.q: Jo's metal toaster has a fault, and the live wire touches its metal case. The case is earthed. What does the earth wire do?
opts: Carries current to ground, so a fuse or breaker acts
Stops current reaching the ground, so the case stays safe
Compares live and neutral currents, then cuts the power
Lowers the case's voltage, so the fuse is not needed
b.why: The earth wire joins the case to the ground, giving the fault current a safe path. That large current blows the fuse or trips the breaker, which cuts the power. Comparing the live and neutral currents is the job of a residual current device, not the earth wire.
b.clue: Picture the easiest path the fault current can take.
